summary: A revision to the appendix of BBN Report 1822 that lists sites on the ARPANET, now written to include sites about to join. BBN urged hosts to add new sites to their local address tables quickly. It also argued that a host program should not drop valid messages just because the sender is missing from a table.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC publishes an address list for ARPANET hosts, including sites scheduled to connect soon. It asks hosts to update their local lists and questions whether a missing entry should block communication.

subtitle: A prospective directory of ARPANET host and IMP addresses.

tldr.problem: Hosts needed address information for sites that were connected or about to join the ARPA Network.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 208 revises an appendix of BBN Report 1822 and lists host and IMP numbers, network addresses and scheduled installations.
tldr.outcome: The note urges hosts to add new sites to their local tables and questions rejecting otherwise valid messages solely because an address is missing from a table.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 208 as Unknown and records no RFC that updates or obsoletes it. The RFC is an address-table revision for the ARPA Network in 1971.

sections.title: Why Publish a Prospective List
sections.content:
The document attaches a revised Appendix A of BBN Report 1822. It is the first attempt described in the RFC to make the site list prospective, including sites scheduled to connect in the near future.

The reason is that many hosts apparently require a site's address in a local table before their NCPs permit communication. The note urges those hosts to add new sites as soon as possible and announces a planned BBN address change on September 1.
sections.plainLanguage: The list includes sites expected to join, not only sites already connected. Hosts that need local address entries are asked to add the new ones early.

sections.title: How the Address Is Formed
sections.content:
For most Host-to-IMP and IMP-to-Host messages, bits 9 through 16 of the message leader carry a network address. In a Host-to-IMP message, it identifies the destination host; in an IMP-to-Host message, it identifies the originating host.

The address combines two bits for a host number attached to an IMP with six bits for the IMP number. The table gives decimal IMP numbers, host numbers and network addresses, along with planned installation dates for hosts not yet connected.
sections.plainLanguage: A network address combines a host number with the number of the IMP it connects through. The table lists those numbers for current and planned hosts.

sections.title: Address Tables and Message Handling
sections.content:
The note argues that an NCP should not discard an otherwise valid message only because the sender's address is absent from a local table. It makes a similar point about preventing a user from trying to contact a remote site whose address the user knows.

The RFC states this as the author's view; the address appendix itself provides the listed assignments and scheduled installations.
sections.plainLanguage: The author questions blocking a valid message just because a local address list does not contain its sender. The note also questions stopping users from trying an address they know.
